items.title: Ed Sheeran Says Dropping Macklemore From Tour Was ‘Promoter’s Decision, Not Mine,’ Explains Why He’s Not Speaking Out on Israel and Palestine
items.summary:
Ed Sheeran has broken his silence on Macklemore's removal from the U.S. leg of his Loop tour, saying in a lengthy statement that the call came from elsewhere. "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran wrote, noting that the rapper's contract for the run was with the promoter rather than with him.

The dispute began when Macklemore used his opening sets at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4 and 5 to say "Free Palestine" from the stage and perform "Hind's Hall," his song about the pro-Palestine occupation of a Columbia University building, while footage of the destruction in Gaza played on the stadium screens. The Israeli American Council circulated a petition demanding his removal, arguing the event "was an Ed Sheeran concert — not a political rally." Messina Touring Group, which promotes the U.S. dates, announced Monday that Macklemore would not appear on the remaining support slots after venues said they would not host shows with him on the bill.

Sheeran said he spent the week in talks with venues, promoters and activists on both sides trying to find a resolution, and that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was among the people he spoke with. As Variety reported, Sheeran's statement follows Macklemore's own account on Monday, in which the rapper accused Kraft of rallying fellow stadium owners against him, and a separate response from Kraft. Sheeran said he was told the venues' position rested on how Macklemore delivered part of his message rather than on its substance.

Much of the statement addressed why Sheeran does not use his own shows to discuss the conflict. "I am not complicit," he wrote, saying he holds personal views on the war and supports causes privately. He pointed to the makeup of his audience — "young people, often children, of all backgrounds" — and said he respects Macklemore's "strength of purpose" while arguing that "there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace."

Macklemore had been booked for eight of the ten remaining dates, including Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta and Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis. Sheeran said he would not abandon fans who had made plans or the crew and other musicians who depend on the tour for work. The Loop tour resumes Sept. 19 in Philadelphia.

items.title: Bob Dylan Somehow Finds 371 Unreleased Songs for Another Rolling Thunder Box Set
items.summary:
Bob Dylan's archival operation has another enormous release on the way. Rolling Thunder Revue: The 1976 Live Recordings, a 39-disc box set collecting 371 unreleased songs, arrives Nov. 6 and covers the second leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue, which ran in spring 1976.

The set includes every professionally recorded show from that leg, which accounts for nearly all of them. Dylan's bands across the run featured Rob Stoner, Scarlet Rivera, Howie Wyeth, T Bone Burnett and Mick Ronson, the guitarist from David Bowie's Spiders From Mars. Guests on the tour included Joan Baez, Joni Mitchell, Willie Nelson and Allen Ginsberg.

One show is being carved out for its own release: the May 16 concert in Fort Worth gets a standalone 3xLP on the same day, and "Going, Going, Gone" from that night is available now. Pitchfork noted that the full tracklist is posted on Dylan's website rather than reproduced in full, which is understandable given its length.

The 1976 box follows the 2019 collection devoted to the tour's 1975 leg, which arrived alongside Martin Scorsese's Rolling Thunder documentary. In a press release, Burnett made a large claim for the tour's influence: "The Rolling Thunder Revue was the first national punk rock tour. It opened a door that led to a furious explosion of new music — the Clash, Elvis Costello, the Ramones, the Sex Pistols, and on and on. Dylan had done it again. He is good at walking through doors that no one else even sees, doors that others think are walls."

items.title: Wednesday Announce Deluxe Bleeds With Demos, Remixes, & Covers
items.summary:
Wednesday are marking the first anniversary of Bleeds with an expanded edition of the album. The North Carolina band's deluxe version arrives Friday, Sept. 18, on Dead Oceans, adding demos, remixes and covers to the 12-song record they released a year ago this week.

The additions include a fresh batch of demos, among them "June 2 (Early Version)," produced by Kenneth Blume, who also worked on the new Weezer album that features Wednesday's Karly Hartzman. Remixes come from Avey Tare, DJ Sabrina The Teenage DJ, Fire-Toolz and Andy Loebs, and the tracklist also carries covers of Wednesday songs by Gouge Away and Joe Harvey-Whyte.

"June 2 (Early Version)" is out now as the first preview. Stereogum described it as starting in the prettier, lower-key register of the band's sound before working toward distorted catharsis, and it closes with a spoken passage from Hartzman: "You killed yourself alone/ In a storage unit/ You'd seen enough/ You knew you had to do it."

The expanded tracklist runs 20 songs, opening with the original album sequence from "Reality TV Argument Bleeds" through "Gary's II" before moving into the new material, which includes a demo of "Poison the Sound" and Fire-Toolz's take on "Bitter Everyday." Pre-orders and pre-saves are open now.

items.title: Angine de Poitrine Make US TV Debut On Fallon
items.summary:
Angine de Poitrine made their first appearance on American television Monday night, performing on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. The costumed Canadian duo, who play microtonal math rock, had already made their UK television debut in June.

The band's profile grew sharply over the past year, driven largely by clips from their KEXP session that circulated widely online. Their Fallon slot went to a new song that has not appeared on any of their albums, titled "Zugzegk" — a name Fallon pronounced, as Stereogum put it, as essentially a wordless clearing of the throat.

In Stereogum's account of the performance, the polka-dotted pair leaned into slinky, playful guitar work that suggested the soundtrack to a surreal surf-rock cartoon, keeping the momentum up from start to finish. It is the kind of set that translates dense musicianship and theory into something an audience can simply enjoy, which is much of why the group broke out in the first place.

items.title: Prime Video in Talks to Take Over Emmys Telecast
items.summary:
The Television Academy is in talks with Prime Video about moving the Primetime Emmy Awards telecast to the Amazon-owned streamer. Sources confirmed the discussions to The Hollywood Reporter, which noted that a deal would mark the first time in Emmys history that the ceremony did not air on a broadcast network.

The timing is not coincidental. The academy's eight-year agreement with ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC expired Monday night with NBC's broadcast of the 78th Emmys. The four networks have rotated the show among themselves since the mid-1990s.

Prime Video already has a foothold in awards programming, holding rights to the Academy of Country Music Awards since 2021, and it has built out a substantial live-events operation through sports deals with the NFL, the NBA and WNBA, and NASCAR. Those two lines of business make a three-hour live ceremony a manageable proposition for the streamer.

An Emmys deal would make the show the second of the four EGOT ceremonies to leave network television. The Oscars are heading to YouTube in 2029 under a five-year agreement with the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which means the Emmys would likely reach streaming first.

The rest of the awards calendar is shifting in other directions. The Grammys move to ABC next year with simulcasts on Hulu and Disney+, while CBS is two years into a five-year deal with the Golden Globes. The network's 10-year run with the Tony Awards ended this year.
